pairs.rationale: Both feeding accounts begin with a water journey and withdrawal. Mark explicitly names a private boat trip to a deserted place; John names the Sea of Galilee/Tiberias. Their location descriptions remain distinct.
Both describe crowds following Jesus in a healing context. John attributes following to previously seen signs; Matthew describes following on foot and Jesus subsequently healing their sick.

The later again-to-the-mountain notice recalls this initial mountain setting. Jesus first sits with disciples; later He withdraws alone because of the crowd's royal intentions. The notices do not independently attest each other.
Both explicitly mark the Jewish Passover's nearness. John 2 introduces a Jerusalem journey; John 6 places the notice in the Galilean feeding setting. No identical year or journey is inferred.
Both feeding scenes discuss buying bread for the crowd. John has Jesus question Philip; Mark has the disciples question buying after Jesus tells them to provide food. Speakers and sequence differ.

Both provision settings include testing. Deuteronomy explains Israel's wilderness testing, hunger and manna; John explains Jesus' question testing Philip before the feeding. This compares the pattern, not identical tests or an independently attested motive.
Both mention two hundred denarii for bread. Philip calls it insufficient for even small portions; Mark's disciples ask whether to buy that amount. Their questions and judgments differ.
Both identify Andrew as Simon Peter's brother and Jesus' disciple. John 1 specifies his earlier hearing from the Baptist; John 6 introduces his contribution to the feeding discussion.
Both feeding accounts specify five loaves and two fish. John additionally names a boy, barley and small fish and questions sufficiency; Mark reports the disciples' inventory after Jesus asks.

Both provision stories involve barley loaves, a question about feeding many, and ensuing abundance. Elisha's story uses twenty loaves for a hundred; John uses five with fish for thousands. The quantities, people and provisions differ.
Both arrange about five thousand men to recline. Luke names groups of about fifty and narrated compliance; John names much grass. The organization details are not silently transferred.

Both describe taking loaves, blessing or thanksgiving, and distributing bread and fish. Mark specifies breaking and giving through disciples; John describes Jesus distributing as much as wanted, without that mediation clause here.
Both narrate satisfied eaters and gathered leftovers. John quotes Jesus' instruction that nothing be lost; Mark records the collection without independently stating that command.
Both report twelve baskets of fragments. John identifies the five barley loaves; Mark additionally mentions fish among the leftovers. Their descriptions remain intact.

The crowd's identification of the Prophet is compared with the promised prophet like Moses from Israel's brethren. Deuteronomy supplies expectation background, not a judgment on every political assumption of this crowd.

Both place Jesus alone on a mountain after feeding. John specifies avoiding forcible kingship; Matthew describes dismissing the crowd and praying. No prayer or royal attempt is inserted into the other account.

Both move the disciples toward their post-feeding water journey. John describes evening descent to the sea; Matthew describes Jesus sending them ahead in a boat. The initiative and timing notices differ.

Both separate the disciples' boat journey from Jesus on land as evening comes. John names Capernaum and darkness; Mark names Bethsaida and Jesus' mountain prayer. No reconstructed route erases the destination difference.
Both describe wind disturbing the disciples' boat journey. John says the strong wind stirs the sea; Matthew describes opposing wind and waves battering the boat.

Both describe rowing difficulties, seeing Jesus walking on the sea and fear. John measures twenty-five or thirty stadia; Mark specifies the fourth watch and His intention to pass them. Details are not merged.
Both give Jesus' It is I and do not fear reassurance during the sea encounter. Mark additionally says take courage.

Both resolve the sea encounter. John records willingness to receive Jesus and immediate arrival; Matthew explicitly narrates boat entry, calming wind and worship. Those actions are not independently asserted by both units.

The place notice explicitly recalls eating bread after the Lord's thanksgiving, narrated earlier with distribution. It identifies that feeding, not independent evidence of the arriving Tiberias boats or every observer's knowledge.
Jesus refers to the crowd's eating and satisfaction, narrated in the feeding account. His present explanation of their motive is additional; the earlier narrative does not itself ascribe that motive.

Both contrast ordinary provision with Jesus' enduring life-giving gift. John 4 contrasts renewed thirst with eternal-life water; John 6 contrasts perishing food with eternal-life food. The Father's seal is additional here.

Both ask what response is required and receive a faith-centered answer in context. John asks about God's works; the jailer asks about salvation and is told to believe Jesus. The questions and household promise differ.
Both direct belief toward Jesus. John calls believing the One God sent God's work; Acts names the Lord Jesus and promises salvation with the household. Their formulations and audiences differ.
Both ask Jesus what sign He performs or shows. John 6 seeks a basis for belief after bread teaching; John 2 challenges His temple action. The requests do not imply identical occasions or motives.

The bread-from-heaven citation corresponds to the psalm's manna and heavenly bread given to the people. John introduces the ancestral wilderness meal; the psalm narrates God's provision in its wider history.

Exodus identifies the Lord as promising bread from heaven while instructing Moses. John contrasts Moses with the Father's giving of true heavenly bread. Exodus does not itself identify that bread as Jesus.

Both join heavenly descent with life and salvation for the world. John 3 names the Son of Man and God's given Son; John 6 calls the descending One God's bread. The images and surrounding comparisons differ.
Both hearers ask Jesus for His offered provision. The crowd asks for bread always; the woman asks for water to avoid thirst and drawing. The gifts, hearers and responses are distinct.

Both promise life-giving provision that removes thirst. John 6 also joins bread, hunger, coming and belief; John 4 uses an eternal-life spring. Neither passage is rewritten as ordinary bodily immunity.
Both contrast exposure to Jesus or His signs with unbelief. Here Jesus addresses the bread-discourse hearers; John 12 gives a later narrative summary. The groups are not automatically identical.
Both connect the Father's gift with Jesus' protection of His own. John 6 speaks of coming and not being cast out; John 10 uses sheep, eternal life and hands from which none snatches.
Both subordinate Jesus' own will to the will of His Sender. John 6 adds heavenly descent; John 5 places the statement in His explanation of hearing and judging.

Both address preservation of Jesus' followers from loss. John 6 states the Father's will for those given and last-day raising; John 17 describes guarding them in the Father's given name and explicitly excepts the son of destruction. The exception is not erased or explained away.

Both connect believing Jesus with eternal life and resurrection. John 6 names the Father's will and last day; John 11 names Jesus as resurrection and life and addresses living despite death. Settings and formulations differ.

Both bread-related settings include grumbling. Exodus' people complain to Moses and Aaron over food; John's hearers grumble over Jesus' heavenly-bread claim. The motives, people and claims are not identical.

Both audiences invoke Jesus' being Joseph's son. Luke places it amid hometown wonder; John adds known parents and objection to heavenly descent. These are reported reactions, not independent biological-paternity conclusions.
Both discourage grumbling. Jesus addresses this bread-discourse complaint; Paul instructs community conduct without grumbling or disputes. The audiences and immediate reasons differ.
The later saying explicitly recalls the necessity of the Father's enabling approach to Jesus. Here the verb is draws and resurrection is added; later the expression is given from the Father.

The God-taught saying corresponds to Isaiah's promise concerning taught children. John applies hearing and learning from the Father to coming to Jesus; Isaiah's addressed children and peace language remain its own wording.

Both distinguish unique divine sight or revelation from general human sight. John 6 says the One from God has seen the Father; the prologue names the only-begotten God making Him known. Titles and expressions are preserved.
Both say belief is joined with eternal life. John 3 explicitly names the Son and adds disobedience and remaining wrath; the shorter John 6 assurance does not repeat those clauses.

Jesus repeats the explicit I am the bread of life identification. The earlier saying continues with coming, believing and absence of hunger and thirst; those additions are not inserted into this shorter unit.

Both recall ancestors eating and nevertheless dying. The later conclusion repeats that contrast against the bread giving enduring life; this is a repeated teaching, not independent historical attestation.

Both describe descending heavenly bread, eating and life beyond death. The next unit identifies Jesus as the living bread and adds His flesh for the world. The added explanation is not silently inserted here.

Both connect given bread with Jesus' body or flesh for others. Luke gives the supper's body-given-for-you and remembrance words; John gives flesh for the world's life. Distinct scenes and terms do not settle every ritual interpretation.

Both questioners ask how Jesus' life-giving teaching can be physically understood. Nicodemus asks about returning to a womb; this group asks about flesh to eat. Their images, identities and subsequent explanations remain distinct.

Both teachings connect Jesus' body or flesh and blood with consumed provision. Luke narrates supper bread and covenant cup; John states the need to eat and drink for life. The wording and setting are not made identical.

Both promise eternal life and raising on the last day. Here the terms are eating flesh and drinking blood; earlier they are beholding the Son and believing. The stated actions are preserved rather than automatically substituted.

Both relate Christ's body or flesh and blood to shared food and drink. Paul names bread and the blessing cup as participation; John calls flesh true food and blood true drink. Neither account supplies all the other's expressions.

Both describe mutual remaining in Jesus and His followers. John 6 connects it with flesh and blood; John 15 uses vine, branches and fruit. The images are not turned into identical physical descriptions.

Both describe life in the Father-Son relation. John 5 names the Father's gift of life-in-Himself to the Son; John 6 names living because of the living Sender and adds the eater living because of Jesus.

This conclusion reprises the contrast between ancestors who ate and died and Jesus' heavenly bread giving enduring life. The earlier units contain that contrast and identify His flesh, without independently attesting another discourse.
Both place Jesus teaching in a Capernaum synagogue. Mark explicitly names a Sabbath entry; John identifies the bread discourse's venue without that Sabbath notice. The occasions are not identified.

Both address difficulty hearing Jesus' teaching. Here disciples call the saying hard; later Jesus challenges opponents' inability to hear His word. Speakers, audiences and explanations are not made identical.

Both portray Jesus knowing people beyond a supplied human report. John 6 describes His inward awareness of disciples' grumbling; John 2 explains His knowledge of people. No mechanism or universal judgment on all followers is inferred.
Both connect the Son of Man with ascent and prior heavenly origin. John 3 explicitly names heaven and descent; John 6 asks about ascending where He was before. No extra elapsed timeline is supplied.

Both explicitly say the Spirit gives life. Paul contrasts Spirit with the killing letter; John contrasts Spirit with unprofitable flesh and calls Jesus' words spirit and life. Their distinct contrasts are preserved.

Both narrators explicitly describe Jesus knowing His betrayer. John 6 additionally names prior knowledge of unbelievers; John 13 explains not all are clean in the footwashing scene. The descriptions are not assigned indiscriminately to every follower.

Jesus' for-this-reason explanation recalls the earlier no-one-can-come saying. Here coming must be given from the Father; earlier the Father draws and Jesus promises resurrection. The different verbs remain visible.

John 6 narrates disciples ceasing to walk with Jesus after the discourse; John 8 defines true discipleship through remaining in His word. The comparison does not supply an unrecorded verdict or motive for every departing person.

Peter credits Jesus with words of eternal life; Jesus later explains His Father-given speech and calls the Father's command eternal life. The confessing disciple and Jesus' explanation are different voices.

Both identify Jesus as God's Holy One. Peter's collective confession of belief differs from the unclean spirit's recognition and confrontation. The shared title does not equate the speakers' faith or occasions.

Both identify danger from one within Jesus' group. Here one of the chosen Twelve is called a devil, with the next unit identifying Judas; later Jesus says one will betray Him. The sayings and occasions differ.

Both identify Judas son of Simon Iscariot in the betrayal narrative. John 6 anticipates his handing Jesus over; John 13 narrates the morsel and Satan's entry. The later actions are not inserted into the earlier notice.

Both narrate efforts to kill Jesus. John 5 gives the opponents' Sabbath and Father-language concerns; John 7 explains His avoiding Judea. The notices concern the narrated opponents, not every Jewish person.
John names the approaching Booths festival; Leviticus prescribes its days and holy gatherings. The law supplies festival background, not this visit's date or an unstated water ceremony.

The brothers argue against acting secretly while seeking publicity; Jesus later goes to the feast not openly but as in secret. This contrasts the stated proposal and narrated manner of travel, not independent events.
John reports His brothers' unbelief at this stage; Acts later includes His brothers in the praying company after the ascent. The passages do not identify each brother or date a change of response.
Both sayings describe Jesus' unfulfilled timing. John 7 says time; John 2 says hour. The words, hearers and occasions are preserved rather than assigned one date.

Both associate opposition with disclosure of evil deeds. John 7 says the world hates Jesus' testimony; John 3 describes evildoers avoiding and hating the Light. The subjects and imagery are not identical formulations.

This unit says I am not going up because the time is unfulfilled; the later narrative records His going after His brothers, secretly. No not-yet word or unrecorded explanation is inserted into the earlier statement.
Jesus' secret arrival contrasts with His brothers' argument for public display. The earlier proposal is not treated as the narrator's assessment of His motives or as an independently narrated trip.

Both report people seeking Jesus at a feast and questioning His presence. John 7 concerns Booths; John 11 concerns Passover and asks whether He will come. The occasions and possible motives are not merged.

Both describe conflicting evaluations of Jesus. Here good versus misleading; later demon-possession versus words and healing inconsistent with that charge. Different speakers' claims are reported rather than endorsed.

Both describe fear restricting favorable public speech about Jesus. John 9 specifies parents and synagogue expulsion for confessing Christ; John 7 does not independently state that particular sanction.
Both place Jesus teaching in the temple. John specifies midway through this feast; Luke describes daily teaching in the later Jerusalem setting. No shared visit or complete timetable is inferred.

Both report amazement at Jesus' understanding in temple settings. Luke concerns a twelve-year-old listening and questioning; John concerns an adult whose study background is questioned. Ages, roles and occasions differ.
Both attribute Jesus' teaching or speech to His Sender rather than Himself. John 12 explicitly names the Father's speech-command; John 7 speaks of the teaching's ownership.

Both connect committed response with knowing truth. John 7 concerns willingness to do God's will and discerning teaching's source; John 8 concerns remaining in Jesus' word, discipleship and liberating truth.

Both contrast self-directed human glory with God's. John 7 tests a speaker by seeking the Sender's glory; John 5 discusses receiving human glory and coming in the Father's name. Their immediate arguments differ.

Jesus invokes Moses' Law while challenging the intent to kill Him. The command against murder supplies concrete legal background; it does not independently narrate this plot or every alleged law violation.
Both contain a demon accusation against Jesus. John 7 combines it with denial of a killing plot; John 8 adds Samaritan and Jesus' denial while honoring His Father. The speeches and settings differ.

Read with7:23's Sabbath-healing explanation, the one-work reference corresponds to the earlier man's restoration on a Sabbath. The earlier scene does not independently record the present audience's reaction.

Genesis gives Abraham the circumcision covenant and eighth-day instruction before Moses. John expressly distinguishes the fathers' origin from Mosaic regulation and discusses Sabbath practice, which Genesis does not explicitly describe here.

Leviticus prescribes eighth-day circumcision; Jesus invokes keeping circumcision law while defending Sabbath healing. The legal verse does not itself narrate this healing or explicitly adjudicate that controversy.
Both require righteous judgment instead of partial assessment. Leviticus names favoritism toward poor or powerful people; John forbids judging by appearance in the Sabbath controversy.

The residents' question about the intended victim corresponds to the earlier narrated intent to kill Jesus. The connection does not make every resident share that intent or independently establish their private knowledge.

Both emphasize Jesus speaking openly. The later trial statement describes public teaching in synagogues and temple; here residents wonder about rulers' response. Public teaching is distinguished from the earlier secret journey.

Both objections rely on perceived knowledge of Jesus' earthly origin. John 6 invokes known parents against heavenly descent; John 7 invokes known origin against a claimed Messiah expectation. The expectations remain speakers' claims.
Both distinguish Jesus' divine sending from coming on His own initiative. John 8 frames love and God's fatherhood conditionally; John 7 challenges the hearers' knowledge of the true Sender.
Both give Jesus distinctive knowledge of the Father or Sender. John relates it to being from Him and sent; Matthew also describes mutual Father-Son knowledge and revelation to others.

Both explain failure to seize Jesus by His hour not yet coming. John 8 locates its saying at the treasury; John 7 follows temple origin-and-sending teaching. They are recurring notices, not one event.

Both describe many believing in Jesus in relation to signs at a feast. John 7 includes the crowd's question about greater future signs; John 2 names belief in His name. Their groups and maturity are not presumed identical.
Both name chief priests and Pharisees arranging Jesus' seizure. John 7 sends officers; John 11 seeks information about His whereabouts. The methods and occasions differ.
Both speak of Jesus going to the One who sent Him. John 7 adds a little time longer; John 16 addresses disciples and their failure to ask His destination.

Jesus later explicitly recalls telling the Jews that where He goes they cannot come and applies the saying to disciples. The changing audience is preserved, without imposing identical or permanent exclusion on both groups.

The question repeats Jesus' immediately preceding seek/not-find and cannot-come saying. This identifies the quoted statement, not an independent verification of the hearers' proposed destination or future events.

Both invite thirsty people to receive provision. Isaiah summons them to water and freely obtained food and drink; Jesus invites coming to Him and drinking. John does not name Isaiah or repeat the full invitation.

Both describe flowing living water. Zechariah locates it in Jerusalem; John relates rivers from his belly to believing in Jesus. The comparison does not identify the sources or prove this is John's sole scriptural referent.

Both relate Spirit reception or outpouring to Jesus' glorification or exaltation. Acts describes the exalted Jesus receiving the Father's promise and pouring it out; John's Spirit-was-not-yet wording is retained rather than expanded.
Both crowds identify Jesus as truly the Prophet. John 6 follows the bread sign; John 7 follows the water discourse. The speakers and occasions are not assumed identical.

Both scenes question Jesus through perceived geographic origin. Nathanael questions Nazareth; the feast crowd questions Galilee and divides over Christ identification. The characters' premises are not endorsed as the narrator's geography.

The crowd invokes Bethlehem as the ruler's expected origin; Micah addresses Bethlehem and announces Israel's ruler from it. The target supplies background for the claim, not John's independent narration of Jesus' birthplace.

The crowd's Davidic-seed expectation corresponds to God's promise of David's seed and an enduring throne. Samuel does not name Bethlehem in these units or state this crowd's knowledge of Jesus' genealogy.
Both explicitly report division over Jesus. John 7 concerns Messiah and origin claims; John 9 concerns Sabbath observance and healing signs. The divided groups are not automatically identical.
Both describe efforts to seize Jesus without completed custody. John 7 says no one laid hands on Him; John 10 says He went out from their hand. The exact circumstances are not made identical.

The officers' return and question about not bringing Jesus refer back to their earlier seizure commission from priests and Pharisees. The later notice reports failure to complete it, not another independently attested arrest mission.
Both describe exceptional response to Jesus' speech. Officers say no person spoke this way; Mark's hearers marvel at authoritative teaching unlike scribes. The listeners and settings differ.

The Pharisees' led-astray question repeats the misleading accusation voiced in the crowd's earlier debate. Different speakers use the charge; neither occurrence makes it the narrator's judgment about Jesus.

The rhetorical question about rulers' belief is compared with the later report of many rulers believing but fearing public confession. Different times and public/private responses do not establish when each ruler first believed.

Both record disparagement of people favorable to Jesus. Here the crowd is called accursed and law-ignorant; later a healed man is called sin-born and unfit to teach. The reported accusations are not endorsed.
The earlier Nicodemus visit identifies this returning participant as a Pharisee and ruler who came at night. This does not make his later legal question a record of every earlier belief.

Moses directs judges to hear disputes and judge righteously without partiality. Nicodemus invokes prior hearing and knowledge before judgment. The rule supplies background, not a proved verbatim citation of a particular statute.

The double-bracketed John sequence sends Jesus to the Mount of Olives. Luke describes His lodging there at night during a Temple-teaching period. The shared movement does not establish the same night or the same narrative setting.

Both describe Jesus teaching in the Temple and people coming early to hear Him. John gives a particular dawn arrival and seated teaching within its double-bracketed sequence; Luke summarizes a recurring daily pattern.

John identifies the woman's alleged offense as adultery; the saved Exodus command prohibits adultery. This supplies the law's moral background, not this woman's identity, the evidence against her, or the prescribed penalty.

The accusers appeal to Moses concerning stoning. Deuteronomy orders death for both adulterous parties and, in its betrothed-city case, stoning of both. John does not supply all those case conditions or authorize restricting the law to women alone.

Both narratives explicitly describe a question meant to trap or test Jesus. Matthew concerns tax and a verbal snare; John's question concerns adultery and accusation, with ground-writing absent from Matthew. These are different confrontations.

Deuteronomy requires multiple witnesses and the witnesses' hands first in an execution. Jesus calls for the sinless person among these accusers to cast the first stone. The shared first-action imagery does not make Deuteronomy itself require sinlessness.

John repeats Jesus' writing on the ground, previously described as with His finger. Exodus describes stone tablets written with God's finger. This is a possible writing-and-law imagery comparison; John never identifies what Jesus wrote or equates it with the tablets.

Jesus tells both addressed people to sin no more. John 8 follows the accusers' departure and His refusal to condemn the woman; John 5 follows healing and includes a warning of something worse. The people and forms of deliverance differ.

Both join life and light against darkness in the presentation of Jesus. The prologue speaks through creation and Word imagery; John 8 speaks of following Jesus as the world's Light. The prologue's continuation is retained rather than detached from its preceding clause.

The opponents' self-witness objection repeats the earlier self-witness/not-true formulation. In John 5 Jesus states a conditional before discussing other witnesses; in John 8 opponents make the charge and Jesus answers it. The speakers and argumentative settings differ.

Both describe Jesus knowing where He comes from and where He goes. John 8 makes that knowledge a ground for His testimony; John 13 places coming from God and returning to God before the foot-washing. These are different scenes.

Both contain Jesus' statement that He does not judge in the described situation. John 8 contrasts His hearers' judgment according to flesh; John 12 explains His saving mission and the word's last-day judgment. This does not erase the Gospel's other judgment sayings.

Both ground Jesus' judgment in His relationship to the Father who sends Him. John 8 says He is not alone and His judgment is true; John 5 speaks of hearing, righteous judgment, and seeking the Sender's will. The explanations are related but differently worded.

Jesus invokes the law's two-person testimony rule. Deuteronomy says one witness is insufficient and two or three establish a matter. John's formulation is not a claim that any two agreeing people automatically speak factual truth.

Both identify the Father who sent Jesus as bearing witness about Him. John 8 also names Jesus' own testimony; John 5 adds that its hearers have not heard the Father's voice or seen His form. The witness lists are not identical.

Both link knowing Jesus with knowing the Father. John 8 answers a question about where His Father is; John 14 answers Philip's request to be shown the Father and uses seeing language as well. Knowing and seeing are not silently made identical expressions.

Both explain a failed attempt to seize Jesus by saying His hour had not yet come. John 8 locates teaching at the treasury; John 7 belongs to an earlier confrontation. This is an internal repeated explanation, not independent attestation of one arrest attempt.

Jesus again speaks of going away, being sought, and hearers being unable to come where He goes. John 8 adds dying in their sin; John 7 speaks of not finding Him and going to the Sender. The warnings retain their different wording.

Both report hearers proposing an explanation for Jesus' inaccessible destination. John 7 asks about the Greek Dispersion; John 8 asks about suicide. These reported guesses are not endorsed as the narrator's account of Jesus' destination.

Both contrast an origin from above or heaven with an earthly origin. John 8 applies above/below and world language directly to Jesus and His hearers; John 3 contrasts the heavenly One's testimony with speech from the earth.

Both connect unbelief with an adverse outcome. John 8 speaks of dying in sins unless the hearers believe that Jesus is 'I am'; John 3 speaks of judgment and belief in the only-begotten Son's name. Their distinct identity formulas are preserved.

Both connect God's truth and sending with the words Jesus speaks. John 3 describes accepting testimony and the sent One speaking God's words; John 8 describes speaking to the world what He heard from the true Sender. Their surrounding judgment and Spirit statements differ.

Both narrator comments explicitly state that Jesus' hearers did not understand. John 8 concerns His reference to the Father; John 10 concerns a sheep-related figure of speech. This is an internal narrative pattern with different subjects and occasions.

Both use Jesus' being lifted up in relation to His mission. John 12 explicitly explains the expression as indicating the manner of His death; John 8 links lifting up the Son of Man with recognition and His Father-taught speech. The explanations are not word-for-word duplicates.

Both affirm that Jesus is not alone because the Father is with Him. John 8 adds that He always does what pleases the Father; John 16 contrasts the Father's presence with the disciples' coming abandonment. The human circumstances differ.

Both narrator reports describe many believing in Jesus. John 8 follows His speech; John 2 concerns signs at Passover. The comparison does not identify the groups or assign every person's subsequent history or quality of faith.

Both link remaining in Jesus or His words with discipleship. John 8 says remaining in His word marks true disciples; John 15 describes His words remaining in the disciples, prayer, and fruit glorifying the Father. The conditional formulations differ.

Both connect the reception of teaching with freedom in a discussion of sin's slavery. John speaks of knowing the truth and being freed; Romans speaks of heartfelt obedience, freedom from sin, and service to righteousness. Neither passage is reduced to a claim about civil status alone.

Both concern Abraham's offspring and servitude. Genesis predicts descendants' oppression and enslavement in a foreign land; John's hearers assert that they have never been slaves. The comparison does not settle whether their claim concerns personal status or ancestral history.

Both depict sin as a form of slavery. Jesus speaks of the person committing sin as sin's slave; Paul discusses obedience, sin leading to death, and transfer into service of righteousness. Their arguments are related without being identical accounts of human bondage.

Both use household imagery to distinguish service from the Son's position. John contrasts the slave's nonpermanence with the Son remaining; Hebrews contrasts Moses' faithful service with Christ as Son over the house. John does not explicitly identify its slave with Moses.

Both attribute freedom to the Son or Christ. John speaks of being truly free after describing sin's slavery; Galatians urges standing in Christ's freedom rather than a yoke of slavery in its own argument. John's saying is not rewritten as the whole Galatian controversy.

Jesus acknowledges Abrahamic descent here while confronting an intention to kill Him. The later exchange qualifies Abrahamic child-language by Abraham's conduct and contrasts it with killing a truth-speaker. This internal argument distinguishes acknowledged descent from the conduct being disputed.

Both ground testimony in what the heavenly speaker has seen or heard. John 8 specifically names what Jesus saw with the Father and then contrasts His hearers' action and their father. John 3 does not supply all the father-language of this confrontation.

Both qualify Abrahamic child-language beyond a bare descent claim. Jesus appeals to doing Abraham's works; Galatians speaks of faith and the blessing of the nations. The criteria's different wording is retained rather than substituting Paul's formulation for Jesus' words.

Both challenge an intention to kill Jesus in relation to an ancestral authority. John 7 invokes Moses and the law; John 8 invokes Abraham and Jesus' God-heard truth. These are different appeals within different confrontations, not a denial of every hearer's ancestry.

Both use one-Father and God language. Malachi appeals to shared divine creation and covenant faithfulness; John's hearers claim God as their one Father, a claim Jesus then tests by their response to Him. The comparison does not endorse their every assertion or invent an accusation about Jesus' birth.

Both connect love for Jesus with His coming from God or the Father. John 8 tests the hearers' claim of divine fatherhood by whether they love the sent Jesus; John 16 speaks to disciples who have loved Him and believed His origin. The audiences and conditional directions differ.

Both connect difficulty receiving Jesus' speech with hearing or stumbling. John 6 reports disciples asking who can hear the hard saying; John 8 has Jesus challenge opponents' inability to hear His word. The groups and stated responses are different.

Both describe the devil in relation to the beginning and moral parentage; the Epistle also describes Cain's murderous conduct as from the evil one. John 8 explicitly adds lying and a murderer from the beginning. This is a moral-character comparison, not a hereditary judgment on an ethnicity.

Both connect speaking truth with an adverse response. Jesus says His hearers do not believe Him because He tells truth; Paul asks whether telling truth has made him their enemy. The speakers, communities, and described reactions differ.

Jesus challenges His hearers to convict Him of sin. First Peter explicitly describes Christ committing no sin and having no deceit, within an account of suffering without retaliation. A rhetorical challenge and the Epistle's positive testimony are distinct forms of speech.

Both link being from God with hearing testimony and not being from God with not hearing. In the Gospel Jesus speaks of God's words; the Epistle speaks of hearing its 'us' and distinguishing truth from error. The speakers and immediate objects of hearing are not collapsed.

Both report a demon accusation against Jesus. John 8 also includes the Samaritan insult; John 7 asks who seeks to kill Him. These are reported hostile claims in different exchanges, not narrator endorsements.

Both join the honor of the Son and Father. John 8 has Jesus deny a demon accusation and contrast His honoring the Father with His hearers' dishonoring Him; John 5 says all should honor the Son as the Father. The forms of the claims differ.

Both distinguish glory connected with God from human honor. John 8 says Jesus does not seek His own glory and another seeks and judges; John 5 says He does not receive human glory and challenges mutual human praise. Seeking and receiving are preserved as different expressions.

Both connect receiving Jesus' word with life beyond death. John 8 says keeping His word means never beholding death; John 5 joins hearing and believing the Sender with eternal life and passage from death to life. The expressions are not reduced to bodily immortality during ordinary earthly life.

Genesis narrates Abraham's death after a life of 175 years, the ancestral fact invoked by these hearers. It does not endorse their demon accusation. Their 'taste death' formulation also differs from Jesus' preceding 'behold death' wording.

Both pose a greater-than-our-father question about Jesus and a patriarch. John 8 invokes Abraham and dead prophets; the Samaritan woman invokes Jacob and his well. The different speakers, patriarchs, and life-giving images remain distinct.

Both speak of the Father glorifying Jesus. John 8 contrasts the Father's glory with worthless self-glorification; John 17 asks the Father to glorify the Son so the Son may glorify Him. The later prayer is not presented as this controversy's immediate event.

Both contrast Jesus' knowledge of His Sender with His hearers' lack of knowledge. John 8 adds keeping the Father's word and the falsehood of denying that knowledge; John 7 adds being from the Sender and being sent. These are internal related claims, not independent witnesses.

John singles out Abraham's joy at seeing Jesus' day. In its patriarchal discussion Hebrews describes faithful people seeing and welcoming unreceived promises from afar. This is a forward-looking faith comparison, not identification of a particular Genesis vision or a claim that Hebrews explicitly names Jesus' day here.

Both report human age markers concerning Jesus: these hearers say He is not yet fifty, while Luke says about thirty at the beginning. They describe different moments and neither makes fifty His age or fixes the year of this exchange.

Jesus contrasts Abraham's coming into being with His own 'I am'; the prologue describes the Word already being in the beginning and creation coming into being through Him. This is an internal preexistence comparison, not a substitution of the prologue's wording for Jesus' exact saying.

Jesus' absolute 'I am' can be compared with God's self-designation to Moses. Exodus gives a fuller designation and Moses' commission. This is a possible divine-name allusion, not an assertion that the two passages contain an identical complete English formula.

Both describe opponents taking up stones against Jesus. John 10 explicitly supplies a blasphemy accusation; John 8 follows the Abraham exchange and describes Jesus hiding and leaving. John 10's spoken accusation is not imported as a quotation into John 8.

Both begin an encounter between Jesus and a blind person. John specifies blindness from birth and Jesus noticing the man; Mark locates its encounter at Bethsaida and has others bring a blind man. Mark does not identify its man as congenitally blind.

Both raise a proposed connection between suffering and exceptional guilt. John's disciples ask about the man or his parents; Luke reports Jesus challenging conclusions about killed Galileans and tower victims. The particular conditions and subsequent warnings differ.

Both resist transferring guilt simply through parent-child relationship. Ezekiel distinguishes each person's responsibility; Jesus rejects the offered explanations of this blindness and points to God's works. John does not say the man and parents never committed any sin or explain every disability.

Both urge action while day or light remains available against approaching darkness. John 9 speaks of doing the Sender's works and night when no one can work; John 12 speaks of walking and believing in the light. The images are not identical timetables.

Jesus calls Himself the world's Light in both. John 9 adds 'while I am in the world'; John 8 describes following Him, avoiding darkness, and having life's light. The temporal clause and the following-language remain distinct.

Both use Jesus' saliva during restoration of sight. John describes mud placed on eyes before washing; Mark describes spitting on eyes and a two-stage laying on of hands. They are different people and procedures, not duplicate details of one cure.

Both healing narratives involve obedience to a directive to wash. John names Siloam, translated Sent, and restoration of sight; Elisha directs Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan for his skin condition. John's man is not Naaman and its procedure is not sevenfold.

Both describe public recognition of a formerly disabled beggar after healing. John concerns a man formerly blind; Acts concerns the man who had sat at the Beautiful Gate and now walks praising God. The healers and disabilities differ.

The neighbors' question about how the eyes opened recurs when the Pharisees ask how the man received sight. The narrator explicitly says they asked again. This is an internal recurrence within one investigation, not a second healing or independent attestation.

The man's account of Jesus making mud, applying it, directing him to Siloam, and his washing and seeing recalls the narrated actions. It is the character's report within this same account, not an independently preserved second record.

Both Sabbath-healing accounts place a healed man under questioning by religious opponents. John 9 says he is brought to Pharisees; John 5 concerns carrying a mat and who commanded it. The people, condition, and immediate disputed action differ.

Both explicitly identify the healing day as a Sabbath. John 9 mentions making mud and opening eyes; John 5 mentions becoming well, walking, and criticism of carrying the mat. The accounts do not give identical procedures or accusations.

The Pharisees' renewed question and the man's mud/washing/sight answer repeat the earlier neighbors' question and his fuller account. The later answer is shorter and does not repeat every earlier detail. This is internal narrative repetition.

Both connect a Sabbath healing with dispute about proper judgment of Jesus. John 7 has Jesus compare circumcision and making a whole man well; John 9 reports divided Pharisaic judgments about Sabbath observance and signs. These are different encounters and arguments.

Both report recognition of Jesus as a prophet after a miracle. John's healed man says He is a prophet because his eyes were opened; Luke's crowd acclaims a great prophet after a dead son is raised. Neither the witnesses nor the miracles are the same.

Both portray authorities confronting evidence of a healing. John's investigators first doubt prior blindness and summon parents; Acts' authorities see the healed man and admit the notable sign cannot be denied. The ailments and initial responses differ.

The parents confirm that their son was born blind, the condition already stated by the narrator. This agreement concerns his earlier condition, not their witnessing the cure. Both statements belong to one literary account and are not independent historical attestations.

Both connect inhibited confession of Jesus with fear of synagogue exclusion. John 9 concerns the healed man's parents and confession as Christ; John 12 concerns believing rulers and fear of Pharisees, with an added glory contrast. The people and stated motives are not identical.

Both use the solemn appeal to give glory to God during questioning. Joshua addresses Achar about his own conduct; John's authorities press the healed man while declaring Jesus a sinner. The verbal correspondence does not endorse that accusation or equate the healed man with Achar.

Both emphasize testimony grounded in personal experience under official pressure. The healed man distinguishes uncertainty about the sinner accusation from knowing he now sees; Acts' apostles insist on speaking what they saw and heard. Their knowledge claims and speakers differ.

The authorities repeat their request for the healing method, already answered in the earlier Pharisaic questioning. This internal recurrence explains why the man next says he has already told them; it does not describe another opening of his eyes.

The earlier answer supplies the explicit report to which 'I told you already' refers. John's later question about wanting discipleship is not evidence that the investigators actually desired to become disciples. The earlier answer and later challenge remain distinct.

The authorities oppose their claimed Mosaic discipleship to the man's association with Jesus. Earlier Jesus argues that believing Moses would lead to believing Him. The contrasting claims are preserved rather than endorsing the reviling or treating Moses himself as a false teacher.

Exodus narrates the Lord speaking with Moses, providing background for the authorities' first claim about God speaking to him. It does not attest their dismissal of Jesus or settle the claimed ignorance of His origin. Moses' conversation remains its own scene.

Both connect Jesus' extraordinary works with the question of His origin from God. The healed man marvels that the authorities do not know His origin despite his opened eyes; Nicodemus explicitly reasons that Jesus' signs require God's presence. The speakers' formulations differ.

The healed man's prayer argument resembles Proverbs' contrast between the ungodly and the righteous person's prayer. John attributes the argument to this speaker; the correspondence does not by itself make it a complete rule excluding every repentant sinner's plea.

Luke's parable supplies a complementary case: a self-confessed sinner asks God for mercy and goes home justified. This qualifies any indiscriminate reading of the healed man's prayer maxim. The tax collector's repentant plea is not the same situation as the accusation against Jesus.

Isaiah promises opened blind eyes and hearing for deaf ears. The healed man emphasizes the unheard-of opening of eyes blind from birth. This is restoration-promise background; Isaiah does not itself specify congenital blindness or assert the exact historical claim made in John.

Both infer God's involvement from Jesus' works. The healed man says someone not from God could do nothing; Nicodemus says no one could do these signs unless God were with him. The from-God and God-with-him formulations are related but not identical.

John 9 describes the man being cast out after his testimony; the later discourse warns followers of synagogue exclusion and further persecution. Chapter9's earlier exclusion policy gives context, but this verse is not expanded into a stated legal procedure or the man's death.

Both connect the Son of Man with belief. John 9 asks the found man whether he believes in the Son of Man; John 3 speaks of that figure's lifting up and eternal life in relation to belief. The saved Son-of-Man title is not replaced with another textual variant.

Both have Jesus identify the expected figure with the One speaking to the hearer. John 9 answers about the Son of Man and adds having seen Him; John 4 answers the woman's Messiah expectation. The exact self-identification pattern does not erase the different titles or scenes.

Both describe worship directed to Jesus after a miraculous encounter. The healed man says he believes; Matthew's boat occupants acclaim Him as God's Son after the water episode. The people, prior miracle, and spoken confession differ.

Both present a reversal in spiritual understanding. John uses seeing and blindness in a judgment saying; Luke records Jesus acknowledging the Father for hiding things from the wise and revealing them to infants. The metaphors differ and neither comparison treats physical disability itself as moral guilt.

Both exchanges associate Pharisaic criticism with blindness imagery. In John some nearby Pharisees ask whether they too are blind; in Matthew offended Pharisees are followed by Jesus' blind-guide saying. The episodes and the extent of each reported group remain distinct.

Both connect knowledge with responsibility. John challenges a claim to see and says sin remains; Luke distinguishes greater and lesser punishment according to a servant's knowledge. Luke still assigns some punishment to ignorance, so the sayings are not made identical exemptions from accountability.

The later explanation gives the thief's destructive purpose, clarifying the earlier unauthorized entry image. Jesus contrasts that purpose with His own life-giving mission. This is one discourse's developing figure, not a second record of a historical burglar.

The introductory figure distinguishes the legitimate shepherd; Jesus later identifies Himself as the Good Shepherd. This internal identification does not require assigning every door, entrant, and doorkeeper detail a single fixed personal equivalent.

Both describe sheep hearing the shepherd's voice. The introduction concerns his own sheep being named and led out; the later saying concerns other sheep being brought into one flock. The doorkeeper is not independently identified with a named biblical person.

Both join the shepherd's voice with the sheep following. Here the sheep know his voice; later Jesus says He knows His sheep. The direction of each knowledge statement is preserved within the recurring figure.

Refusal to follow an unfamiliar voice is related to the later statement that the sheep did not hear the thieves and robbers. This internal explanation does not supply a list of historical strangers or claim every earlier prophet was a thief.

Both explicitly discuss figurative speech. The narrator says the hearers did not understand the sheep figure; the later Jesus contrasts His figures with coming plain speech about the Father. These are different teaching settings, not a rule that every image is unintelligible.

Both make Jesus the means of access through a personal image. John 10 calls Him the sheep's Door; John 14 calls Him the Way and says no one comes to the Father except through Him. Door and Way remain distinct metaphors.

Jeremiah condemns shepherds who destroy and scatter God's sheep; John speaks of thieves and robbers whom the sheep did not hear. This is related counterfeit-leadership imagery, not an identification of every earlier God-sent messenger with the thieves.

Both use flock-provision imagery. John's sheep find pasture through Jesus as the Door; the Psalm describes the Lord's shepherding, nourishment, and restful water. The pastoral background is compared without treating Door and shepherd as one unchanging allegorical role.

Both contrast the flock's good with exploitative leadership. Ezekiel's shepherds consume milk, use wool, and slaughter the fattened animal while failing to feed and care for the sheep; John's thief steals, slaughters, and destroys, against Jesus' abundant life. These are related destructive figures, not a fixed roster of identities.

Both describe Jesus giving His life for others. John uses the Good Shepherd and His sheep; Mark uses the Son of Man's service and a ransom for many. The images and beneficiary expressions are not silently interchanged.

Both depict vulnerable sheep scattered and exposed to predators when care fails. Ezekiel describes wandering sheep without a shepherd; John describes a hired worker fleeing a wolf. The absence of care and the particular form of failure differ.

John explains the hired worker's flight by lack of care for the sheep. First Peter urges willing, eager shepherding rather than base gain or domination. This is a contrast of pastoral motives, not a blanket declaration that every paid worker is uncaring.

Both describe the Lord's knowledge of those belonging to Him. John says Jesus knows His own and they know Him; Second Timothy's seal says 'The Lord knew those who are His' and adds departure from unrighteousness. The present and past formulations and reciprocal clause remain distinct.

Both affirm mutual Father-Son knowledge. John uses it in relation to shepherd-and-sheep knowledge and Jesus' self-giving; Matthew also speaks of the Son revealing the Father. Neither is a verbatim repetition of the other's full argument.

Both use one-shepherd language. Ezekiel names David as ruler and speaks of one shepherd over all in Israel's restoration setting; John promises other sheep hearing Jesus and one flock, one shepherd. John says flock rather than fold here, and this comparison does not itself identify every group of sheep.

Both relate Jesus to the raising of His own body or the taking of His life again. John 2 interprets the sanctuary saying as about His body and later resurrection; John 10 speaks of laying down life, taking it again, and the Father's love. Their images differ.

Both discuss authority concerning Jesus' death. John 10 states His own authority to lay down and take His life under the Father's command; John 19 makes Pilate's claimed authority dependent on a grant from above. Voluntary self-giving does not erase the human agency reported in the Passion.

The renewed division recalls the earlier division over the Sabbath healing and whether Jesus could be from God. John 10 concerns His present words and ensuing demon dispute. This is the Gospel's recurring divided response, not two independent accounts of one conversation.

Both report an accusation that Jesus has a demon. John 10 adds madness and a question about listening; John 7's crowd asks who seeks to kill Him. These are hostile speakers' claims, not narrator affirmations.

The question about opening blind eyes recalls the earlier narrated healing with mud and washing. The later speakers use such a work against the demon accusation. Their rhetorical question is not an independently preserved account of a second healing.

First Maccabees narrates the altar's rededication and the annual eight-day observance beginning on the twenty-fifth of the ninth month. This supplies background for John's feast of Dedication. It does not narrate Jesus' visit or fix its year from the Maccabean date.

Both locate a scene at the portico named Solomon's. John has Jesus walking in the Temple; Acts has Peter, John, the healed man, and an astonished gathering. The named setting is shared, while the participants and occasions differ.

Both report a demand that Jesus say whether He is the Christ. John places it at the feast of Dedication; Luke places it in the Passion interrogation and records His reply about unbelief and unanswered questions. These are different confrontations.

Both describe Jesus' works as testimony about Him in relation to the Father. John 10 speaks of works done in the Father's name; John 5 speaks of works given to complete and testifying that the Father sent Him. The giving and name-language are preserved separately.

Both explain lack of reception through relationship language. John 8 speaks of not hearing God's words because one is not from God; John 10 speaks of unbelief because the hearers are not His sheep. The comparison does not supply a separate account of how one becomes a sheep.

The personal sheep-and-voice statement recalls the opening figure's hearing and following. The earlier sheep know the shepherd's voice; here Jesus says He knows them and they follow Him. Their different directions of knowing are retained.

Both connect eternal life and the preservation of those given by the Father. John 6 speaks of losing none and last-day raising; John 10 speaks of never perishing and no snatching from Jesus' hand. The preservation images are related without replacing their particular words.

John 10 says 'What My Father has given Me is greater than all' and speaks of protection in the Father's hand. John 17 explicitly describes people given to Jesus and belonging to the Father. This compares giving and belonging without changing John 10's grammatical subject to the Father.

Both use Father-Son oneness language. John 10 briefly says 'I and the Father are one'; John 17 describes reciprocal indwelling and prays for believers' unity. The related language is not made an exhaustive definition of every sense of 'one' in the earlier saying.

Taking up stones again recalls the earlier attempt after the Abraham exchange. John 8 describes Jesus hiding and leaving the Temple; John 10 pauses for His response about works. They are recurring hostile actions within one Gospel, not independent accounts of the same attempt.

Both controversies connect Jesus' relationship to the Father's work with an intention to kill Him. John 5 concerns Sabbath work and equality with God; John 10 asks which good work warrants stoning. The next reply's charge and the earlier narrator's explanation retain their different settings.

Both report God-related grounds for hostility toward Jesus. John 5 describes His calling God His own Father and making Himself equal to God; John 10 quotes the accusation of a man making himself God. The Sabbath issue occurs explicitly in John 5 rather than this reply.

Jesus quotes the Psalm's 'you are gods' wording. The Psalm also calls its addressees sons of the Most High. John calls this written text Law in the argument; the comparison does not supply a definitive identity for every addressee called a god.

Both affirm Scripture's enduring force in Jesus' teaching. John says Scripture cannot be broken while discussing its god-language; Matthew speaks of fulfilling the Law and Prophets and no iota or stroke passing before accomplishment. Their claims and formulations are related, not identical quotations.

Both connect consecration with sending into the world. John 10 names the Father consecrating and sending Jesus; John 17 prays for the disciples, compares their sending with His own, and describes Jesus consecrating Himself for them. The agents and recipients of consecration remain distinct.

Both present works associated with the Father as grounds for testimony concerning Jesus. John 10 states the negative condition: if He does not do the Father's works, do not believe Him. John 5 positively describes given works testifying to His sending.

Both connect the works with Father-Son indwelling, but John 10 urges belief in the works so the hearers may know and continue to know that indwelling; John 14 urges belief in the indwelling or because of the works. John 14 also distinguishes Jesus' speech from the Father's indwelling works. This is a close internal recurrence of reciprocal language, not independent historical attestation.

Both describe a hostile attempt against Jesus ending in His departure. Luke has a crowd lead Him toward a precipice before He passes through them; John says they seek to seize Him and He leaves their hand. John's unstated escape method is not supplied from Luke.

The return to John's earlier baptism site recalls the named Bethany beyond the Jordan. Both concern the Baptist's location; this Bethany is not automatically identified with the later Bethany associated with Martha and Lazarus. The later return is internal narrative retrospection.

The crowd's assessment recalls the Baptist's earlier testimony about Jesus, including the Lamb and Spirit witness. John 10 explicitly says John performed no sign; the Spirit's descent witnessed in John 1 is not a miracle performed by John. Both reports belong to this Gospel.

Both settings join testimony about Jesus, His presence among the people, and many believing. Samaria has the woman's witness followed by hearing Jesus; beyond the Jordan the preceding verse recalls John's witness. The witnesses and communities are not identified with one another.
